  "text": "The week before her father moved into the flat, Nora came to empty his shed. He had agreed that most of it could go.

“Except the useful things,” he said.

She held up a bicycle pump with no hose.

“There’s a hose somewhere.”

He sat beside the doorway while she sorted flowerpots, paint tins, and lengths of wood too short to mend anything. Each time she opened a drawer, he leaned forward.

At the back of the workbench she found a jam jar full of keys. Some were labelled in her mother’s handwriting: SIDE GATE, METER, OLD PADLOCK.

“Can these go?”

He took the jar and shook it once, as though the sound might help him decide.

“The brass one fits your grandmother’s house.”

“That house was demolished.”

“I know which house it was.”

She turned back to the bench. Outside, a neighbour’s mower stopped, leaving the shed suddenly quiet.

After a while he began putting keys on the upturned lid. He made two piles, then combined them.

Nora carried another box to the car. When she returned, the jar was empty except for a small silver key.

“What’s that one?”

“Your old money box. The red one.”

“I haven’t got it anymore.”

He nodded and tipped the key into his palm.

At the flat that evening, she unpacked his kettle and put milk in the fridge. He was trying the back-door key in a kitchen drawer.

“This one locks,” he said.

She watched him open it again. Inside lay the small silver key.

“Good,” she said. “You’ll know where it is.”"
